Talks, posters, and figures carry the same research as a paper,
but the reader sees them for less time and cannot reread them.
This chapter gives practical rules for each.

## Guidelines for slide decks {#sec-slide-deck-guidelines}

When preparing slides for a lab meeting,
conference, qualifying exam, or thesis defense,
follow these guidelines:

- **Always include slide numbers**:
  Slide numbers make feedback specific.
  During questions or a practice run,
  listeners need to refer back to a slide quickly
  (e.g., "On slide 14, how was that variable defined?")
  instead of describing it or guessing where a topic occurred.
- **Complete, record, and review practice runs**:
  Before any significant presentation,
  rehearse the complete talk out loud,
  record the practice run (with screen recording software, a webcam, or your phone),
  and watch the recording.
  The recording shows your pacing, timing, filler words, and transitions,
  and whether slide text and figures stay legible on screen.
- **One main point per slide**:
  Limit the cognitive load of each slide.
  If a slide presents several findings or a complex argument,
  split it across consecutive slides so the audience can follow each point.
- **Prefer visual evidence**:
  Audiences cannot read dense paragraphs while listening to a speaker.
  Use clean charts, diagrams, and annotated figures instead of text-heavy bullet lists.
- **Ensure high contrast and readability**:
  Use large fonts and high-contrast colors.
  Check that axis labels, legends, and annotations can be read
  from the back of a large room or on a low-resolution projector.

## Presentation and poster resources {#sec-presentation-resources}

- How to tell a compelling story in scientific presentations [@kirchoff2021]
- The science of storytelling: the David Attenborough style of scientific presentation [@ratcliff2023]
- [How to create a better research poster in less time](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1RwJbhkCA58) -
  Mike Morrison's video introducing the #betterposter template
- [Towards an "#evenbetterposter"](https://mitcommlab.mit.edu/be/2023/09/27/toward-an-evenbetterposter-improving-the-betterposter-template/) -
  the MIT Biological Engineering Communication Lab's improvements to that template

## Scientific figures {#sec-scientific-figures}

A clear figure lets a reader check a result without help from the text.
Before you share a figure:

- Label the x-axis and y-axis clearly.
- Use panel labels when a figure has several subplots.
- Include enough tick marks and tick labels.
- Print tick labels as plain or comma-separated numbers, such as 0.001 or 10,000, not in scientific notation.
  When the numbers are huge or tiny, rescale the units and say so in the axis title, such as "dollars (millions)".
- Use font sizes that are easy to read without dominating the plot.
- Use colorblind-friendly palettes
  (see [ColorBrewer](http://colorbrewer2.org/) or [iwanthue](https://medialab.github.io/iwanthue/)).
- Define colors, shapes, and line types in a legend.
- Minimize abbreviations in labels and legends.
- Use transparency to show overlapping data.
- Show measures of precision, such as 95% confidence intervals.

For more:

- Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures [@rougier2014]
- [Tufte CSS](https://edwardtufte.github.io/tufte-css/) -
  style HTML articles like Edward Tufte's books and handouts,
  with sidenotes, typography, and tight integration of graphics with text
